high_priority_articles.summary: ASML Raises South Korea Lithography Spare Parts Prices 10%, Pressuring Samsung and SK Hynix as AI Expansion Boosts Equipment Makers' Pricing Power  TradingKey
high_priority_articles.full_text:
ASML will uniformly raise replacement parts prices for EUV and DUV lithography equipment in South Korea by 10%, effective January 2027. This hike increases operating expenses for Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, while reflecting growing pricing power among semiconductor equipment suppliers amid AI-driven capacity expansion. ASML's after-sales business, representing a significant revenue share, is expected to benefit from this adjustment. Similar pricing pressures are emerging across the industry, driven by robust equipment demand and rising component costs, though the ultimate profit impact depends on customer negotiation dynamics and ongoing supply-demand conditions.
TradingKey - According to South Korean media outlet The Elec, ASML (ASML) will uniformly raise the prices of replacement parts for lithography equipment supplied to the South Korean market by 10%, with the new prices taking effect for deliveries starting in January 2027 and covering all spare parts for extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machines.
This price hike will increase equipment maintenance costs for Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, while also reflecting that semiconductor equipment suppliers are seeking greater pricing power against the backdrop of AI-related capacity expansion.
According to reports, ASML headquarters submitted price hike proposals to Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix through its South Korean branch in early September, which were finalized after negotiations with the procurement departments of both companies.
This price adjustment covers both consumables requiring regular procurement and key components needed when equipment fails or experiences performance degradation. For installed lithography systems, continuous operation relies on maintenance and spare parts replacement; therefore, the price increases will not only affect new purchases but also raise the operating expenses of existing equipment.
Unlike past price adjustments made in response to rising costs or procurement difficulties for individual raw materials, this uniform 10% price hike is relatively rare. Industry insiders believe that widespread increases in component costs are one reason, and ASML also seeks to boost its own profit margins as customer profitability improves.
However, a 10% rise in spare parts procurement prices does not imply a corresponding 10% increase in customers' overall equipment operating costs or chip manufacturing costs. The actual impact depends on replacement frequency, procurement structure, and the share of related costs.
ASML categorizes services for its installed equipment base—such as maintenance, upgrades, and spare parts replacement—as a standalone business line. Data cited in reports indicates that revenue from this business reached nearly 8.2 billion euros in 2025, accounting for about 25% of total revenue. The company expects related revenue to potentially grow by over 30% in 2026.
As customers' installed equipment base expands and production activity increases, demand for maintenance and upgrades is expected to keep growing. If implemented smoothly, the price increase on spare parts will provide additional support for related revenue and help the company absorb part of the upward cost pressure.
However, spare parts represent only one component of this business, and this price adjustment is limited to the South Korean market. Therefore, it cannot be extrapolated that ASML's global aftermarket revenue or profit will increase by a corresponding 10%. The extent of profit improvement will still depend on cost changes, procurement volumes, and product mix.
Regarding complete systems, earlier reports also indicated that ASML planned to raise tool prices, but TSMC had explicitly opposed it. The diverging progress of these two types of price adjustments shows that equipment vendors' pricing power must still be assessed based on product category and customer negotiation dynamics.
Price adjustments have already extended to other semiconductor equipment suppliers. Applied Materials (AMAT) previously disclosed that prices for both new and existing products have increased, while Tokyo Electron also stated that it is responding to rising costs through price adjustments.
On the demand side, investments in AI chips, High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), and advanced nodes are driving capacity expansion among memory makers and foundries, increasing procurement demand for equipment, spare parts, and production consumables.
According to SEMI forecasts, global semiconductor equipment sales will reach $165.9 billion in 2026, up 23.2% year-on-year; by 2028, the market size is expected to grow to $229.5 billion.
Amid rising equipment orders and tightening supply for certain components, the scope for customers to leverage procurement scale to push down unit prices may narrow. However, whether price increases can continue to be passed through still depends on the supply-demand dynamics of different equipment types and the pace of customers' capacity expansion.
For ASML, the key focus moving forward is whether price hikes can translate into profit growth for its aftermarket business; for customers such as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, they need to absorb the pressure of rising equipment maintenance and procurement costs while expanding capacity and raising capacity utilization rates.

high_priority_articles.title: What has Trump’s Board of Peace achieved in a year since Gaza ‘ceasefire’? - Al Jazeera
high_priority_articles.summary: What has Trump’s Board of Peace achieved in a year since Gaza ‘ceasefire’?  Al JazeeraIn three years, Israel's war on Gaza hasn't just changed the Middle East, it's changed the world | Steve Bloomfield  The GuardianChild among eight killed by Israel on Gaza ‘ceasefire’ anniversary  Al Jazeera'Every day there is killing': Gazans face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls  BBCA US-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the war in Gaza. A yea...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
It has been one year since United States President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace (BoP) brokered a “ceasefire” aimed at eventually ending Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza.
However, rather than receiving relief and a chance to rebuild, Palestinians in the enclave continue to face attacks and be uprooted as Israeli forces have expanded control within the territory.
Trump first proposed the BoP in September 2025, saying it would stabilise Gaza and ensure lasting peace.
In November, a United Nations Security Council resolution recognised the board as a “transitional administration” in Gaza.
But what has the board achieved? Here’s what we know:
What were the BoP’s goals?
The BoP’s mission was laid out in Trump’s 20-point Gaza peace plan, as was the “ceasefire” between Israel and Hamas. The ceasefire began on October 10, 2025.
The plan envisioned steps for each side to take that could eventually create a “credible pathway” to Palestinian statehood.
It required Israeli forces to withdraw to about 50 percent of the Gaza Strip and cease aerial and artillery bombardments. It also required Israel to release 250 Palestinian prisoners and another 1,700 people jailed from Gaza since October 7, 2023, the day that Hamas led attacks into southern Israel and Israel began the war. The plan proposed reopening border crossings to allow much-needed aid into Gaza.
The peace plan required Hamas to release all Israeli captives. It also proposed a later phase in which the group would disarm and its members would be granted amnesty or a safe exit from Gaza.
The peace plan established the BoP as a transitional governing body until the Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the occupied West Bank, could take over.
An International Stabilization Force (ISF), led by the US, was supposed to take over security in Gaza from withdrawing Israeli forces, the plan stated. It also proposed the reconstruction and redevelopment of Gaza, whose people, it said, “have suffered enough”.
What has the BoP done in the past year?
In February, the BoP’s members, who each joined in exchange for a $1bn annual fee, met in Washington, DC, for its first summit, at which member states pledged $7bn in funding although aid agencies said reconstructing Gaza would cost closer to $70bn.
On the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month, the BoP also unveiled a 66-project recovery plan worth $2.4bn.
What has BoP achieved?
The BoP’s achievements are tied to the success of the Gaza peace plan.
Under that, Hamas has released all 168 living captives and Israel has freed Palestinian prisoners.
Hamas has also announced the dissolution of its government in the Gaza Strip although Israel has dismissed that as a “stunt”.
Other goals under the peace plan have been only partially met.
Governance has been hampered. While a National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), meant to act as the governing authority in Gaza, was founded, Israel has not granted it entry into the Strip. The NCAG reports directly to the board and is led by Chief Commissioner Ali Shaath and other Palestinian technocrats. It operates from Cairo. Israel has not stated why the committee is not permitted to enter Gaza.
Aid remains restricted. About 227 aid trucks enter the Strip daily when 600 trucks were supposed to, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) hunger monitor.
Israel has classified thousands of basic items, such as tents and essential equipment like ventilators, as “dual use” items, which means they have military and civilian applications, and has restricted their flow into the Strip. About 1.4 million Palestinians – or most of Gaza’s more than 2 million people – will suffer hunger until at least December, the IPC has noted. That is 200,000 more than those who faced hunger in May, suggesting a significantly deteriorating situation.
What has not been achieved?
Observers argued that the BoP has entirely failed to secure the “ceasefire” as Israeli attacks have continued almost daily on the Strip.
Since October 10, 2025, more than 1,400 Palestinians, mostly women and children, have been killed. In the three years since the war began, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, and thousands more are missing and presumed dead under the rubble.
Israel says its continuing attacks target Hamas members, but the group vehemently denies the claims.
Israel also now occupies about 60 percent of the Strip, more than the 50 percent agreed in Trump’s peace plan. The “Yellow Line”, which demarcates the area of Gaza under Israeli occupation, has been pushed farther into the Strip, causing further displacement and squeezing Gaza’s population into an ever-shrinking area. Palestinians unknowingly crossing the “Yellow Line” have been shot dead.
In December, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said the army “will never fully leave” the Strip.
Mohamad Elmasry at the Doha Institute of Graduate Studies told Al Jazeera that Israel is simply continuing a broader policy of “ethnic cleansing” in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. “They are making life miserable,” he said, adding: “This is all by design.”
Consequently, the BoP has also failed to ensure Hamas disarms so phase two of the peace plan could begin.
Although Hamas has agreed to hand its weapons over to the NCAG, it rejects the “disarmament” clause because Israel has not ceased its attacks or withdrawn from the Strip as agreed. At the same time, Israel has said it will not move forward with the plan if Hamas does not disarm, leaving the two sides in a standoff.
Meanwhile, no stabilisation force has been deployed. Six countries – Indonesia, Morocco, Kazakhstan, Albania, Kosovo and Uganda – have so far committed personnel to form a security force of 20,000 soldiers and 12,000 police headed by the US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM).
There has been no meaningful reconstruction in Gaza. Palestinians continue to live in tent camps infested with rodents and insects with little to shield them from intense heat, or rain.
Will BoP take over from UNRWA?
The Trump administration and BoP have echoed Israel’s rejection of the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, or UNRWA, which has long provided lifesaving humanitarian aid, education, development programmes and social services in Gaza and employs about 11,000 Palestinians.
The BoP said last month that it will not work with UNRWA, essentially sidelining the agency.
A BoP official told The Associated Press news agency that UNRWA could continue working in Gaza if its programmes were deemed relevant but the agency’s “days are over”.
UNRWA said the move was “not logical”.
In June, the UN General Assembly voted overwhelmingly to extend UNRWA’s mandate until 2029. The BoP itself is mandated to oversee the peace process until December 2027 when its progress will be reviewed for possible renewal by the UN.
Analysts and rights groups have raised concerns that the BoP could take over all aspects of Gaza’s rebuilding. Countries too, including France and other European nations, have called out any attempts to replace the UN in the Strip.
But Elmasry said no country is willing to take action. “There are a lot of international actors that do not want to cross the US,” he said. That essentially leaves the fate of more than 2 million Palestinians to Trump, he added.
Ultimately, the BoP has “failed”, said Simon Mabon, a professor at Lancaster University.
“The failure to implement its own plan to end the Gaza conflict demonstrates its impotence and the inability to ensure that Israel and, to a lesser extent, Hamas, remain bound by their own commitments [and] has allowed the genocide to continue,” he concluded.

high_priority_articles.title: [进展] Malaysia’s trade grows 22.4pc in 1h 2026, MOF urges supply chain diversification - Malay Mail
high_priority_articles.summary: Malaysia’s trade grows 22.4pc in 1h 2026, MOF urges supply chain diversification  Malay Mail
high_priority_articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 9 — Malaysia’s trade remained resilient in the first half of 2026 (1H 2026), with total trade rising 22.4 per cent to RM1.795 trillion, but the country needs to strengthen supply chains and diversify its export markets and import sources to cushion future external shocks, the Ministry of Finance (MoF) said.
MoF said Malaysia should move further up the global value chain and reduce its exposure to disruptions abroad to strengthen its competitiveness and economic resilience.
“It is crucial for Malaysia to strategically strengthen trade security and build national resilience against future global disruptions, including exploring new export markets and import sources,” the ministry said in its Economic Outlook 2027 report released today.
Diversifying import sources would help address immediate supply deficits while also creating a more flexible and resilient supply chain, according to MoF.
Malaysia’s external trade remained resilient during 1H 2026, supported by higher trade with major trading partners, particularly China, which grew 30.6 per cent, followed by the United States at 25.7 per cent, Taiwan (34.7 per cent), Singapore (21.5 per cent) and Hong Kong (45.8 per cent).
Nonetheless, MoF said, it is imperative for Malaysia to build a comprehensive and multi-layered trade resilient strategy to achieve domestic sustainability.
“The government is intensifying efforts to accelerate integration and sophistication with higher value-added supply chains to cushion exposure to external shocks, including through technological advancement and domestic innovation,” it said.
The ministry added that Malaysia is charting the path toward attracting high-growth high-value (HGHV) investments, increasing economic complexity and expanding skilled jobs, as well as strengthening the domestic supply chain.
Anchored by the Madani Economy framework and complemented by the 13th Malaysia Plan, 2026-2030, policies including the National Semiconductor Strategy (NSS), New Industrial Master Plan (NIMP) 2030, New Incentive Framework (NIF), National AI Action Plan (2026 — 2030) and National Energy Transition Roadmap (NETR) were formulated to capture greater global value chain.
“These policies prioritise deepening local manufacturing capabilities, accelerating technological innovation and expanding domestic participation in higher value-added segments, particularly within the advanced electronics and semiconductor ecosystem,” it added. — Bernama

high_priority_articles.title: US CPI Preview: Will September Inflation Revive October Fed Rate-Hike Bets? - Markets.com
high_priority_articles.summary: US CPI Preview: Will September Inflation Revive October Fed Rate-Hike Bets?  Markets.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The September US Consumer Price Index could determine whether the Federal Reserve delivers another interest-rate increase in October or waits until December.
Economists expect headline inflation to accelerate as higher gasoline and energy prices feed into the index. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, is forecast to remain more stable and will probably carry greater weight in the Fed’s decision.
The report arrives after US consumer sentiment fell to 46.3 in October while one-year inflation expectations rose to 4.7%. A significant upside CPI surprise would reinforce concerns that energy-related inflation is spreading into the wider economy and could force policymakers to consider consecutive rate increases.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics will publish the September CPI report on Wednesday, October 14, at 8:30 a.m. ET.
It will be the final CPI report before the Federal Reserve announces its next interest-rate decision on October 28. The Producer Price Index will follow on October 15, providing an additional measure of inflationary pressure at the business level.
| CPI Indicator | August Result | September Forecast | 
|---|---|---|
| Headline CPI, month over month | 0.4% | Approximately 0.5% | 
| Headline CPI, year over year | 3.4% | 3.6%–3.7% | 
| Core CPI, month over month | 0.3% | Approximately 0.2% | 
| Core CPI, year over year | 2.4% | Approximately 2.4% | 
| Current federal funds target | 3.75%–4.00% | No change before October 28 | 
The Cleveland Federal Reserve’s inflation nowcasting model projects a 0.53% monthly increase in headline CPI and a 0.20% rise in core CPI. That would place annual headline inflation near 3.6% while leaving core inflation around 2.4%.
Forecasts remain unusually uncertain because gasoline, electricity, travel and other energy-sensitive prices have been volatile throughout September.
Headline CPI increased 0.4% in August after rising only 0.1% in July. The annual inflation rate remained unchanged at 3.4%.
Core CPI rose 0.3% during the month, while the annual core rate eased to 2.4% from 2.5%.
Gasoline prices increased 3.9% and accounted for more than one-third of the monthly increase in the overall index. The broader energy index rose 2.1%, while shelter costs increased 0.3%.
Over the 12 months through August, energy prices climbed 16.3%. Gasoline was 27.4% more expensive than a year earlier, while fuel oil prices increased 52%.
Those figures demonstrate why the Fed is concerned that the current energy shock may last longer than originally expected. If gasoline rose sharply again in September, headline inflation could move further away from the central bank’s 2% objective.
Energy is expected to be the main reason annual CPI rises toward 3.6% or 3.7%.
One inflation model estimates that seasonally adjusted gasoline prices increased approximately 10% in September. That would be considerably larger than August’s 3.9% advance and could push the monthly headline CPI increase toward 0.5%.
Brent crude remained above $100 per barrel during much of the period as conflict involving Iran disrupted shipping and raised concerns about supplies moving through the Strait of Hormuz.
Higher oil prices affect CPI directly through gasoline, diesel, heating oil and airfares. They can also influence food, delivery and manufacturing costs, although those indirect effects normally take longer to appear.
The Fed cannot increase the global supply of oil. Its concern is that a persistent energy shock could influence wages, corporate pricing decisions and household inflation expectations.
The University of Michigan’s October survey showed one-year inflation expectations rising to 4.7% and five-year expectations reaching 3.5%. Both were the highest since May.
A headline CPI increase caused entirely by gasoline may not be sufficient to trigger an October rate hike. Evidence that higher energy costs are spreading into core services would be substantially more important.
Core CPI is forecast to rise 0.2% in September after a 0.3% increase in August.
A 0.2% monthly increase would be relatively reassuring because it would be consistent with gradually moderating underlying inflation. The annual core rate would probably remain near 2.4%.
Investors should examine several individual categories:
The Fed is more likely to look through an energy-driven increase if shelter and core services continue cooling. A broad rise across those categories would create a more difficult policy decision.
The Federal Reserve raised its target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00% in September, delivering its first rate increase since July 2023.
Minutes from the meeting showed unanimous support for the increase. Most officials also believed another move would probably be appropriate before the end of 2026, but there was little support for automatically raising rates at every meeting.
The Fed’s median projection places the federal funds rate at 4.1% at the end of 2026, implying one additional quarter-point increase. Policymakers have not determined whether that move should occur in October or December.
Interest-rate markets currently assign approximately a 19% probability to an October hike. The probability of at least one additional increase by December is around 68%.
Weak September employment data caused investors to reduce expectations for an immediate move. The economy added only 29,000 jobs, giving the Fed a reason to wait and evaluate the effect of September’s increase.
A sufficiently strong CPI report could reverse part of that repricing.
For October hike expectations to rise materially, the report would probably need to show that inflation is broader than gasoline. A core monthly reading of 0.3% or higher, accompanied by strong shelter and services inflation, would provide a much stronger hawkish signal than headline CPI alone.
| Scenario | Possible CPI Result | Likely Fed Response | Potential Market Reaction | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Hotter than expected | Headline at or above 0.6%; core at or above 0.3% | October hike probability rises sharply | Dollar and yields higher; gold and growth stocks lower | 
| Broadly in line | Headline near 0.5%; core near 0.2% | October hold remains favored; December hike stays possible | Initial volatility followed by consolidation | 
| Softer than expected | Headline at or below 0.3%–0.4%; core at or below 0.1% | October hike odds decline further | Dollar and yields lower; gold and technology stocks higher | 
These thresholds are scenario markers rather than official forecasts. Market reaction will also depend on revisions and the composition of the report.
A headline reading of 3.7% or higher would confirm that overall inflation is moving away from the Fed’s target. If core CPI also exceeds forecasts, markets may begin pricing a second consecutive rate increase in October.
A core monthly increase of 0.3% would translate to an annualized pace well above the Fed’s comfort zone, particularly if shelter and services account for the advance.
Headline CPI around 0.5% and core CPI near 0.2% would support the view that the inflation rebound is primarily energy-related.
The Fed would probably leave rates unchanged in October while maintaining hawkish language and preserving the option of a December increase.
A monthly headline reading below 0.4%, combined with core CPI of 0.1% or less, would indicate that the energy shock is having a smaller effect than feared.
Such an outcome could reduce December hike expectations and raise questions about whether September’s increase was the final move of the tightening cycle.
The 10-year Treasury yield finished the latest week at approximately 5.243%, while the two-year yield ended near 4.789%.
Long-term yields recently reached their highest levels in 24 years as investors reacted to persistent inflation, heavy government borrowing and uncertainty surrounding the Fed’s policy path. Strong Treasury auctions subsequently helped yields retreat from their peaks.
A stronger CPI report could push the 10-year yield back toward its recent high above 5.3%. A softer result would probably produce the largest reaction in shorter-dated yields because those securities are more directly influenced by Fed policy expectations.
High yields also increase pressure on equities by raising corporate financing costs and reducing the present value of future earnings.
The dollar has completed four consecutive weekly gains as investors anticipated that US interest rates would remain elevated.
A hot CPI report would probably strengthen the dollar by increasing expectations for another Fed hike. EUR/USD could return toward its recent 17-month low, particularly while the euro remains under pressure from France’s debt crisis.
USD/JPY could move closer to 160 if Treasury yields rise, although the possibility of Japanese currency intervention may limit the advance.
A softer CPI report would weaken the dollar, especially if traders conclude that the Fed can postpone additional tightening until December or abandon another hike entirely.
Gold recovered toward $4,200 per ounce after falling to a two-month low earlier in the week.
The metal faces competing forces. Inflation and geopolitical uncertainty support demand for gold as a store of value, while elevated real yields and a stronger dollar increase the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset.
A stronger-than-expected core CPI reading would probably be negative for XAU/USD in the immediate reaction because it could lift both the dollar and Treasury yields.
A softer report could allow gold to extend its recovery by reducing rate-hike expectations. If headline inflation rises because of energy while core CPI remains subdued, the reaction may be mixed because inflation-hedging demand could offset pressure from higher nominal yields.

high_priority_articles.summary: Samsung & SK hynix Have Set A Dangerous Greed Cycle That Has Trickled Down To Suppliers Like ASML, Who Now Want To Match Their Customers’ Profit Margins  Wccftech
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The profits being raked in by Samsung and SK hynix during the DRAM shortage have made both memory manufacturers the source of envy amongst high-profile suppliers like ASML, which is now reportedly seeking a price hike to match what its clients are generating in annual net earnings. According to the latest report, the changes have been finalized, setting a perilous precedent across the entire industry.
ASML is reportedly charging a flat 10 percent higher fee for every EUV and DUV part, with Samsung and SK hynix seemingly having agreed
The Dutch equipment manufacturer is raising prices for all replacement parts found in its machines. According to The Elec, these changes are expected to take effect in January 2027, with the proposal reportedly sent to both Samsung and SK hynix through their Korean subsidiaries last month. Given the scale at which both manufacturers are generating profits, they likely felt that a 10 percent price hike was a drop in the bucket, so based on the fresh details, they agreed.
Both EUV and DUV equipment have a plethora of moving parts that are susceptible to wear and tear over time. These parts include photolithography equipment, optical paraphernalia such as lenses, mirrors, light sources, and precision actuators. With every single one of these parts obtaining a 10 percent price hike, it’s clear that, being the only manufacturer of advanced EUV machinery, ASML doesn’t wish to get left behind during the AI boom and wants the same opportunity as Samsung and SK hynix when it comes to printing money.
In fact, one unnamed industry source has noted that while prices have risen across an entire spectrum of components, ASML seeks a larger margin to match what its customers, Samsung and SK hynix, are making. The Dutch firm has forecasted that its revenue would increase by more than 30 percent this year, and that’s without the price hike initiated. Additionally, Chinese customers who intend to purchase DUV equipment will also have to pay an additional 10 percent.
Given that the entire industry wants an upper hand in the AI race, these clients have agreed to the hike. While ASML is part of the industry responsible for mass-producing cutting-edge wafers, it hasn’t been adversely impacted by memory and NAND flash shortages, so it’s clear the company wants to capitalize in the same way as Samsung and SK hynix. Unfortunately, this practice has set off a chain reaction spreading through the entire industry.
Companies like Applied Materials and Japan’s Tokyo Electron have increased the price of their products, and with this cycle seeing no end, consumers are going to receive the short end of the stick.

high_priority_articles.title: A U.S.-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the war in Gaza. A year later, progress has stalled - Los Angeles Times
high_priority_articles.summary: A U.S.-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the war in Gaza. A year later, progress has stalled  Los Angeles Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
- Click here to listen to this article
- A year after a U.S.-brokered ceasefire halted major operations and secured the release of all remaining hostages, Israeli strikes continue and Gaza’s 2 million Palestinians remain in limbo.
- The agreement’s broad promises — a new Palestinian administration, an international security force, Hamas disarmament and Israeli withdrawal — have stalled amid deepening disagreements.
- More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since the truce began, and little has been rebuilt as most residents remain displaced in tents, rubble or damaged buildings.
Saturday marked a year since a ceasefire deal brokered by President Trump and Arab allies promised to end the war in Gaza, and Israel is still launching deadly strikes on the devastated territory.
The agreement halted major military operations, freed all remaining hostages and increased humanitarian access. But it has failed to deliver on promises of a new Palestinian administration aided by international forces, the disarmament of Hamas and an end to Israel’s control over more than half the territory. Almost nothing has been rebuilt.
Israel has tied any progress on other issues to Hamas’ complete disarmament, while the militant group — and the Trump administration — say they should happen simultaneously. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hardened his stance over the summer, openly defying Trump, his most important ally, ahead of Israeli elections later this month.
The wrangling has left Gaza’s 2 million Palestinians in limbo. Most are sheltering in rodent-infested tent camps, the rubble of their former neighborhoods or war-damaged buildings at risk of collapse.
In the Jabaliya area of the northern Gaza Strip, Abdullah Abu Zubaida’s family lives in a makeshift shelter built from the debris of their house.
“When the ceasefire began last October, we expected the war to halt, assassinations to cease, and aid to flow in,” he said. None of that has happened.
For Ne’man Abu Jarad and his family, displaced from Beit Lahia in northern Gaza to Khan Yunis in the south, the truce also has brought no clear path home. The family, including five daughters, continues to live in tents.
“The ceasefire is merely nominal, ink on paper,” Abu Jarad said.
Early success raised hopes
The 20-point ceasefire agreement, reached after months of negotiations under the Biden and Trump administrations, ended major military operations and led to the return of all the remaining hostages taken in Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack that ignited the war.
Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people that day and abducted 251. Israel responded with massive bombardment and a ground invasion that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by United Nations agencies and independent experts. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll but says women and children make up around half the dead.
After the deal was announced, Trump called for a new era of harmony in the Middle East. “We have a once-in-a-lifetime chance to put the old feuds and bitter hatreds behind us,” he said at a gathering marking the deal.
The agreement called for much more
The agreement called for Hamas to hand over power to a committee of Palestinian administrators vetted by the Board of Peace, a new body chaired by Trump and charged with implementing the ceasefire.
The militants officially dissolved their government in July but left the civil service intact and remain the dominant power in the roughly 40% of Gaza not controlled by the Israeli military. Israel has meanwhile barred the new Palestinian administration from entering Gaza via Egypt.
The formation of an International Stabilization Force was announced in February but has yet to materialize. Indonesia, which pledged the largest troop contingent — 8,000 soldiers — put those plans on hold last spring as the world’s focus shifted to the Iran war.
Israel was supposed to withdraw from Gaza but has instead seized more territory, pushing the Line of Control, generally known as the Yellow Line, westward toward the Mediterranean Sea. It has also carried out regular strikes on individuals it accused of violating the ceasefire, approaching the Yellow Line or having taken part in the Oct. 7 attack — strikes that have often killed civilians.
Israeli strikes have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians since the ceasefire took effect, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. Sporadic attacks have killed five Israeli soldiers in Gaza in the same period.
More deadlock after Netanyahu defied Trump
In July, Trump announced a deal to disarm Hamas, portraying it as a breakthrough in the long-stalled process.
That deal, an extension of the original ceasefire, called for Hamas to disarm “in a gradual, sequential and time-bound manner” that is “linked to an Israeli withdrawal, in phases.” Hamas confirmed for the first time that it had agreed to disarm, also linking it to Israel halting its strikes and withdrawing from Gaza.
Days later, Netanyahu announced that Israel would not withdraw from any part of Gaza until after Hamas had completely disarmed, explicitly rejecting the agreement announced by Trump.
The rare instance of friction between the two allies came as Netanyahu seeks to shore up his nationalist base ahead of Oct. 27 elections that could end his nearly unbroken 17-year rule, the longest in Israel’s history.
Netanyahu has come under fire over security and intelligence failures leading up to the Oct. 7 attack, with opponents accusing him of having been soft on Hamas. That gives him little space to make even minor compromises on Gaza, at least until a new government is formed, which could take months.
In the meantime, virtually nothing has been rebuilt in Gaza, Hamas is weakened but still in power, and a return to all-out fighting cannot be ruled out.
Krauss writes for the Associated Press. AP journalist Wafaa Shurafa in Jabaliya, Gaza Strip, contributed to this report.

high_priority_articles.title: NATO 3.0 and the Long Road to a European Pillar - Defense.info
high_priority_articles.summary: NATO 3.0 and the Long Road to a European Pillar  Defense.info
high_priority_articles.full_text:
On September 16, 2026, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte delivered the Ditchley Foundation’s 62nd Annual Lecture at Ditchley Park in Oxfordshire. In the house where Churchill once met Roosevelt’s envoys to make the case for Lend-Lease, Rutte set out what he calls “NATO 3.0”: “not a reboot, but a rebalancing of our security for the better,” or, in his own summary phrase, “a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO.”
One line in the speech matters most to me: “To stay transatlantic, NATO is becoming more European.”
I have spent four decades working on that proposition. In 1991 I published The Europeanization of the Alliance, which grew out of interviews across Paris, Bonn, London and Brussels in the late 1980s. Its argument was that the Alliance’s future depended on building a European pillar inside it, not outside it or against it. To hear the Secretary General make that case at Ditchley as official Alliance policy is to be reminded how long the idea took to arrive, and how much had to go wrong before it did.
That is the subject of my forthcoming book, The Western Alliance in Transition: From the Cold War’s End to the Battle for Europe’s Future, the first volume in a four-volume series on the Alliance. Reading Rutte’s speech against the book is instructive.
The speech describes the destination. The book explains the route, and why the journey took so long.
Three Eras, or Five Phases?
Rutte tells NATO’s history in three eras. NATO 1.0 “stood its ground, held the line, and pushed back against the brute force of the Soviet Union.” NATO 2.0 “started at this ‘end of history,'” and was “marked by the move away from the territorial defence of Europe to ‘out of area’ operations,” while “defence budgets declined, and military power dwindled across Europe.” NATO 3.0 is the correction.
As a summary for a lecture, it works.
But Rutte’s NATO 2.0 spans three distinct periods, each with its own logic, and the differences matter.
The first is what I call the structural transformation decade, 1990 to 2001. It was not a pause while the end of history played itself out. It was a period of high-stakes decisions made under real uncertainty, built on three bets: that Russia could be integrated into a cooperative European security framework; that consolidating Soviet nuclear weapons under Moscow’s control would be stabilizing; and that NATO enlargement could proceed without foreclosing the first two. None of these bets was irrational at the time. Each had its own logic, and each its own way of failing.
The second is the expeditionary detour, from 2001 to 2014. After 9/11 the Alliance remade itself as a reservoir of forces for U.S.-led coalitions in Afghanistan, Iraq and Libya. Those operations produced real achievements in deployability and multinational command. They also hollowed out the core mission. Heavy forces shrank, air defenses aged, and the analytical community that should have been tracking Russian military modernization was allowed to atrophy. By 2014 NATO was, as I put it in the book, “institutionally intact but strategically hollow with respect to the one mission its founding treaty was written to perform.”
The third is the partial return to direct defense after Crimea, from 2014 to 2021. The Alliance recognized the problem but could not close the gap between political commitment and military means. Thin stockpiles, fragile supply chains and fragmented procurement limited what governments could do, even once they understood what needed doing.
Then came the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which turned that gap from a seminar topic into a question of survival. What Rutte calls NATO 3.0 grew out of that experience.
The distinction is not academic. If NATO 2.0 was simply an era of complacency, then NATO 3.0 is a recovery of nerve. If it was a sequence of reasonable bets, a costly detour and an incomplete recovery, then NATO 3.0 is something harder: a reckoning with structural tensions the Alliance has managed and deferred, but never resolved.
Where the Speech and the Book Converge
On the substance of what has changed, the speech and the book line up closely.
The burden. Rutte rejects “the casual assumption, made by many, that our biggest friend and Ally would always provide most of the muscle and pick up the bill, no matter what.” The book traces that assumption back further, to the Atlanticized template of American primacy and European dependency set during the Cold War and repeated after 2001, when Washington chose to fight in Afghanistan largely on its own terms, taking allied support selectively.
The geography. Rutte notes that eight of NATO’s nine Forward Land Forces, “from the Black Sea to the Arctic Circle,” are led by European Allies or Canada. In the book I argue that Finland and Sweden’s accession fused the Baltic, Nordic and Arctic theaters into a single strategic space, and that the states closest to Russia have become agenda-setters for the Alliance. Europeanization has not disappeared; it has been redistributed north and east. The resulting structure is arguably more serious militarily than the Franco-German framework it is replacing.
Industry. “Military might and industrial might go hand in hand,” Rutte said. As I read it, that is the central lesson of the Ukraine war. Deterrence now rests as much on factories, power grids, data networks, ports and rail corridors as on brigades and battlegroups. An alliance that cannot move forces across its territory, protect its energy and digital systems, or replace what it uses up in war has not been transformed, whatever its communiqués say.
Ukraine as teacher. Rutte said that “what we are learning from Ukraine is helping strengthen our own defences, including with Ukraine’s expertise in drones and air defence.” Ukraine’s wartime industrial adaptation has made it both partner and teacher for the West, a reversal few in Western capitals expected in 2022.
Plural leadership. Speaking in Britain, Rutte stressed the UK’s role, from the Coalition of the Willing to the deep precision strike initiative and the sharing of Storm Shadow technology with Ukraine. That fits what the book describes as a more plural leadership in European defense: Anglo-French activism, German industrial weight, Polish strategic scale, Nordic seriousness and Baltic urgency. Strategic direction is shared rather than centrally commanded. That may make the system more resilient, but it also means political coherence has to be built continuously.
Integration. Rutte said NATO must be “the engine for this change – turning national investment into common requirements, integrated forces, credible plans, and collective deterrent power.” The least glamorous part of that engine is standardization: the more than 1,300 standardization agreements and allied publications that let thirty-two militaries fight as one force. It rarely makes headlines, but it is what turns political commitment into military capability.
Where the Speech Leaves Questions Open
There are also places where the speech is quieter than the history suggests it should be.
The Russia question. Rutte described Russia’s hybrid campaign against the Alliance as “a sign of weakness, and a symptom of Putin’s failure in Ukraine.” That may be so. But the long effort to integrate Russia, through Partnership for Peace, the NATO–Russia Council and successive resets, failed, and nothing stable has replaced it. The Alliance has found a more credible deterrence posture. It has not found a durable peace. NATO 3.0 answers the military problem Russia poses, not the political question of what European order follows the war.
The European Union. The speech barely mentions the EU, yet the war has shown how much military credibility depends on tools outside NATO’s mandate: industrial policy, energy security, investment screening, infrastructure protection and supply-chain resilience. These are largely EU domains. A more European NATO without a more capable, more strategic EU will reach its limits quickly. The real task is to make the layered system of NATO, the EU and coalitions of the willing work as a system rather than as overlapping bureaucracies.
Political will. The spending figures are striking: a commitment made at The Hague in 2025 to invest 5% of GDP in defense and security by 2035, and, by Rutte’s count, $258 billion in additional investment by European Allies and Canada across 2025 and 2026. But the lesson of the past four decades is that political will in a democratic alliance is never fixed; it must be renewed continually. The real test of NATO 3.0 is not the size of this year’s budgets but whether they are sustained after the immediate shock fades.
The American variable. Rutte was candid about the role of President Trump: “he’s right. We needed this shot of adrenaline.” That is an important admission. Washington’s pressure has driven the transformation as much as Moscow’s aggression. It also points beyond the Alliance itself, to the broader question of how political change within Western societies, the United States included, is reshaping the strategic West. That question lies outside The Western Alliance in Transition, which deliberately stops in 2025, and is the subject of a separate book I am preparing on the transformation of the West.
The transatlantic logic. One of the strongest passages in the speech deserves more attention than it is likely to get. “The Russian nuclear submarines for example coming out of the Kola Peninsula aren’t targeting Europe,” Rutte said. “Their aim in wartime is the destruction of the U.S. homeland.” This is the best answer to anyone in Washington who sees European defense as Europe’s problem alone. Defending the North Atlantic and the Arctic is defending the United States. Commands like Joint Force Command Norfolk, and the growing role of maritime autonomous systems in efforts such as Arctic Sentry, are where that connection becomes operational.

high_priority_articles.title: Airtel Money goes public in London, bringing Africa’s mobile money opportunity to global investors - TechTrendsKE
high_priority_articles.summary: Airtel Money goes public in London, bringing Africa’s mobile money opportunity to global investors  TechTrendsKE
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Airtel Money began conditional trading on the London Stock Exchange on Friday, 9 October, with an implied valuation of £5.3 billion, or about US$7 billion, giving investors a public-market route into one of Africa’s largest mobile money businesses.
The shares were priced at £1.96 each. They opened around that level and rose as high as £2 during early trading, a gain of about 2%, after the offering attracted demand several times greater than the number of shares available. The company’s formal admission to the exchange and the start of unconditional trading are expected on 14 October.
The listing gives Airtel Money a standalone market valuation as it seeks to expand beyond wallet transfers and mobile payments into a wider range of financial services. Its prospects will depend on how effectively it converts its large customer base and transaction volumes into revenue, while expanding digital adoption and merchant payments across its African markets.
Airtel Money shares begin trading in London
The offer price of £1.96 values Airtel Money at approximately £5.3 billion. The initial sale covers 270 million existing shares, with proceeds of about £529 million going to selling shareholders rather than being raised as new capital by the company. An additional 27 million shares may be sold through an over-allotment option. If exercised in full, that would increase the total offer to £582 million.
Airtel Africa is expected to remain a long-term strategic shareholder and retain control of Airtel Money. The listing therefore gives some existing investors an opportunity to sell shares while leaving the mobile money business under its parent group’s influence. The transaction is a secondary share sale, so Airtel Money does not receive the proceeds from the shares sold in the IPO.
The International Finance Corporation, the World Bank Group institution focused on private-sector development, was allocated shares worth £67.2 million under its cornerstone investment commitment. The offer also included an allocation of eight million shares for eligible UK retail investors. Conditional trading is initially restricted to investors who applied for and received shares in the offer, with broader unconditional trading expected to begin after formal admission.
Revenue and earnings give investors a measure of scale
Airtel Money’s valuation rests on an established business with substantial revenue and earnings. For the financial year ended March 2026, the company reported revenue of US$1.355 billion, up 36% from US$994 million a year earlier. Underlying EBITDA, a measure of operating earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, rose 31% to US$689 million. Its underlying EBITDA margin was 50.8%, down from 52.8% in the previous year.
The figures show both the pace of growth and the importance of maintaining profitability as the business expands. Wallet services generated US$648 million in revenue during the year, while payments and transfers contributed US$573 million. Financial services, including offerings such as credit and other financial products, generated US$61 million. These figures indicate that the business remains heavily reliant on core wallet and payment activity, even as it develops additional services.
The company’s transaction volumes have also grown beyond the scale of a conventional person-to-person transfer service. Airtel Money processed about US$213 billion in payments during the 12 months to June 2026, according to figures disclosed for the listing. That figure covers a different reporting period from the financial year ended March 2026, so it should not be directly compared with the full-year revenue figures. The volume nevertheless illustrates the breadth of activity moving through its network.
App adoption offers room to increase customer value
A key growth opportunity is encouraging more customers to use Airtel Money’s smartphone app and digital services. In the six markets highlighted in its IPO disclosures, app customers generated average revenue per user of about US$9.50, compared with US$1.80 among feature-phone customers. The figures suggest that customers using the app can be more valuable to the business, although the comparison does not establish that app usage alone accounts for the difference.
Smartphone users represented about half of Airtel Money’s customer base, but only around 13% of those smartphone customers used the app during the 12 months to June 2026. Airtel Money therefore has room to encourage existing customers to use more of its digital services rather than relying solely on basic wallet functions. The company’s disclosed app transaction value increased from about US$5.5 billion to US$10.95 billion over the period, showing a rise in activity through that channel.
For Airtel Money, higher app adoption could support greater use of payments, transfers and other services. It could also help the company build more frequent customer relationships and lower its dependence on physical agents for some transactions. The commercial outcome will depend on whether customers adopt these services at scale and whether the additional activity produces lasting revenue growth without eroding margins.
Merchant payments and financial services broaden the business
Merchant payments and bill payments are another important part of the company’s expansion. According to figures cited in coverage of the listing, revenue from these services increased by 61% in the 12 months to June 2026. More merchant transactions can give customers additional reasons to keep money in their wallets and use Airtel Money for everyday purchases, while providing businesses with a digital channel to receive payments.
Airtel Money’s network includes about 2.3 million agents and 490,000 merchants, alongside bank integrations and partners connected through its platforms. These relationships extend its reach beyond direct transfers between individuals and create opportunities to support retail payments, bill settlement and business transactions. The scale of the network is an advantage, but the value it generates depends on active usage, transaction economics and the ability to compete for merchant acceptance.
The company is also developing services that sit alongside payments, including credit, savings, insurance and other financial products in selected markets. A planned Mastercard virtual card is another route to connecting wallet balances with online and card-based payments. Such services could increase the number of ways customers use Airtel Money, although product availability and uptake will differ by market and remain important factors in assessing their contribution to earnings.
Competition and customer conversion will shape growth
Airtel Money operates in markets where mobile money is already an established part of daily financial life. In Kenya, it competes with Safaricom’s M-PESA, which has a broad merchant network and a strong position in consumer payments. Other markets also have local payment providers, banks and fintech companies seeking customers and transaction volume. Airtel Money’s opportunity is therefore not simply to add users, but to persuade consumers and businesses to make it a regular payment option.
The company’s existing telecommunications customer base offers a potential route to growth because some Airtel subscribers in its markets do not yet use Airtel Money. Converting those customers into active wallet users could expand its reach without requiring it to acquire every customer from outside the group. However, mobile connectivity and mobile money adoption are different measures, and the number of subscribers does not automatically translate into a comparable number of potential active wallet users.
In Kenya, Airtel Money has also been working to improve the proposition for merchants and consumers through bank integrations, cross-network transactions and initiatives such as Bizna Wallet. These efforts are relevant to its wider strategy because a wallet becomes more useful when customers can pay more merchants, move funds across services and use it for routine financial needs. Their long-term impact will depend on adoption and sustained transaction activity rather than the launch of individual features.
What the listing means for African fintech
Airtel Money’s London listing gives public-market investors a way to assess the financial performance of a large African digital payments business separately from its telecommunications parent. The valuation will be measured against revenue growth, profitability, customer activity and the company’s ability to extend its services beyond basic wallet transactions. Its early share-price movement provides an initial market reference, but conditional trading is not the same as a settled long-term valuation.
The offering also highlights the structure of the transaction. Because the IPO mainly involves existing shares, it provides liquidity for selling investors rather than a direct injection of new funds into Airtel Money. Airtel Africa’s continued majority ownership leaves the business connected to the wider group while it operates as an independently listed company.
For African fintech, the listing offers a public-market reference point for a business built on mobile money at continental scale. Airtel Money has substantial revenue, a large customer base and high transaction volumes, but its next period of growth will depend on whether it can convert those advantages into more frequent app usage, stronger merchant payments and broader financial-service adoption. Investors will be watching whether that expansion can continue while the company protects its earnings margins and competes in markets where customers already have established alternatives.

high_priority_articles.title: The Real Fear Hanging Over Stocks Isn’t a 5% Treasury Yield but Falling Long Rates on Recession Angst: Analysis - bloomingbit
high_priority_articles.summary: The Real Fear Hanging Over Stocks Isn’t a 5% Treasury Yield but Falling Long Rates on Recession Angst: Analysis  bloomingbit
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Summary
- Brokerages said a drop in long-term U.S. Treasury yields driven by slowing growth would be a bigger negative than a rise in the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield.
- They said the moment short-term yields rise while long-term yields fall would be a key warning sign that the bond market is pricing in the 'fear of R.'
- They said the current short- and long-term yield trend deserves close attention, given that the S&P 500 plunged 24.77% over nine months during the 2022 yield-curve inversion phase.
Forecast Trend Report by Period
A 5% U.S. 10-year Treasury yield isn’t the problem
The return of the fear of "R"
The real problem comes when long-term yields fall on growth worries
In 2022, an inverted yield curve sent the S&P 500 down 24% over nine months
Stock investors are on edge as the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury has climbed above 5%, but brokerage analysts increasingly say a drop in long-term yields could be the bigger threat. If yields fall because the growth outlook is weakening, that could spill into a recession. If short-term yields rise on inflation pressure while long-term yields fall on slowing growth, that may signal the bond market is once again pricing in fear of an "R" — recession.
According to the financial investment industry on October 10, the U.S. Treasury sold 10-year notes at a high yield of 5.300% at an auction held on October 7. That was the highest awarded yield since November 2000. The 10-year Treasury yield in the secondary market also moved above 5% at the close on September 23 and has kept rising, recently trading around 5.3%.
Kim Jun-young, an analyst at iM Securities, said the recent rise in yields has been driven by higher real rates tied to growth expectations. Stocks have been rallying, with the S&P 500 closing at a record 7,818.93 on October 6. It also set an intraday high of 7,844.52. Stock indexes are a leading indicator of the economy.
Kim's view is that investors should be more wary of the moment long-term yields stop rising and begin to fall. Rising yields are not the cause of an expansion but the result of one, he said, adding that rates simply follow growth. A decline in yields caused by fading growth should be read not as a positive but as a warning. Once slower growth starts pulling yields lower, weak economic data may no longer be interpreted as boosting hopes for Federal Reserve easing, but instead as a signal of weaker corporate earnings.
That view also aligns with the market’s traditional reading of short- and long-term yields. In financial markets, short-term yields are typically used as a gauge of monetary policy expectations, while long-term yields reflect the medium- to long-term growth outlook. If inflation strengthens expectations for Fed tightening and pushes short-term yields higher while recession worries drive long-term yields lower, the gap between the two can narrow quickly.
Recent inflation data have already raised concern. The Institute for Supply Management’s manufacturing prices index came in at 77.9, well above the market forecast of 72.9. Its services prices index also rose to 74.0 from 72.6 a month earlier.
Lee Eun-taek, an analyst at KB Securities, said the market begins pricing in Fed tightening when worries about persistent inflation build. In that environment, short-dated Treasury yields can rise quickly. The 2-year Treasury yield climbed 12.34% last month, outpacing the 10-year’s 11.24% increase.
The picture could worsen if signs of slower growth emerge as well. If concerns about cooling AI investment or a broader economic slowdown intensify at the same time, long-term growth expectations would weaken, Lee said. In that case, long-term yields may stop rising and could even fall. The moment short-term yields rise while long-term yields decline could become a key warning signal.
Short-term yields are usually lower than long-term yields. That is because lenders demand additional compensation for the risk of tying up money for longer periods. The spread banks earn by borrowing short from depositors and lending long to companies is one of the industry’s core profit models.
The problem comes when short-term yields rise above long-term yields. If banks become more conservative after that profit model breaks down, money stops circulating smoothly through the economy, which can damage growth. To overcome that kind of environment, a powerful new growth engine, such as technological innovation, needs to emerge.
Investors can look back to 2022. It was the late stage of a boom fueled by loose monetary policy introduced to overcome the Covid-19 pandemic, just as inflation tied to that policy and the Russia-Ukraine war surged with a lag. The Fed raised interest rates sharply to contain inflation, but growth expectations failed to keep pace and stocks stumbled badly. The S&P 500 fell 24.77% in the first three quarters of 2022. The market was able to rebound only after ChatGPT’s release on November 30, 2022, helped revive expectations for growth in the artificial intelligence industry.
Still, Lee said it is not yet time to worry about an inverted yield curve and the return of recession fear. For now, the picture is the opposite. Long-term yields are still rising, while short-term yields have recently pulled back. The 2-year Treasury yield has fallen 0.11 percentage point this month through October 7.

Despite India and the U.S. narrowing their differences, trade talks between the world’s largest nations by economy and population have hit a roadblock. According to BMI, a Fitch Solutions company, a breakthrough in the near future is unlikely as negotiations remain ongoing.
Bilateral trade talks were initiated following a meeting between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and U.S. President Donald Trump in 2025, with the goal of achieving $500 billion in bilateral trade by 2030. By February 2026, New Delhi and Washington had announced a basic framework for an interim trade agreement.
However, in October 2026, Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said that negotiations for a final deal had reached a “plateau,” with further concessions being “very, very difficult” for both nations, according to Reuters. Amid persistent roadblocks and delays, the prospect of an interim trade deal is offering hope for progress in bilateral ties.
“We expect India and the US eventually to conclude a narrow interim trade deal, although the remaining differences make a near-term breakthrough unlikely,” BMI said in a report on the status of the India-US interim trade agreement, according to Business Standard.
Vision Times reporter Venus Upadhayaya spoke with Dr. Ram Singh, Professor and Head of the Centre for Distance and Online Education (CDOE) at the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade in New Delhi, about the causes of the impasse in trade talks and what to expect next.

Vision Times: India and the U.S. are unlikely to see a major advance in trade negotiations in the near future, as the two sides remain split over market access, agriculture, purchase of U.S. goods, and India’s procurement of Russian oil, according to BMI (formerly Business Monitor International), a FitchSolutions company. Can you give us a background of this and help us understand what actually led to this situation?
Dr. Ram Singh: The impasse reflects a shift from tariff bargaining to a broader negotiation over certainty and strategic interests. The February framework narrowed tariff differences, but agriculture, market access and US purchase demands remain politically sensitive for India. Meanwhile, Washington’s pressure over Russian oil—and levy of additional tariff in forms of anti-dumping, CVDs, strategic industry tariffs (steel, copper, aluminium), and threat to complete economic alignment has complicated the bargain.
The US demand for amendments in India GST [Goods and Service Tax], Corporate and digital tax law, domestic subsidies, sectoral caps on FDI, FCRA [Foreign Contribution Regulation Act] and FEMA [Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999] regulations has not gone well with New Delhi. India is seeking meaningful preferential access and tariff certainty, while resisting concessions without reciprocal gains. Thus, the issue is now much beyond tariff certainty to regulatory uncertainty including issues of trust, reciprocity and predictability.
Vision Time: BMI expects trade negotiations to carry on towards the Dec. 14–15 Group of Twenty summit in Miami, which could serve as the next political prop, although it considers an agreement by then unlikely. Why has it been delayed so much? Are their geopolitical factors behind this delay?
Dr. Singh: The delay reflects more than unresolved tariff issues; it reflects a widening strategic trust deficit. India’s trade diversification through deals with the UK, EU, New Zealand, UAE and EFTA has reduced pressure for short-term tariff relief at the cost of strategic autonomy in energy and defence procurement.
Public rhetoric portraying India as a “hell-hole”, “dead economy” or “tariff king”, and its hyphenation with Pakistan, has further strained trust. With the February framework’s unique benefits diluted, and talks now described as “short strokes” and “not imminent”, breaking the deadlock will require substantial political investment by both sides.
Vision Time: While India and the U.S. have narrowed their differences, the remaining issues will be the hardest to resolve, the BMI report observed. All countries have differences on trade issues and that is the case for the U.S. as well. Why is this equation with India so unique?
Dr. Singh: First, agriculture is not uniquely contentious with India; Washington faces similar market-access difficulties with established partners such as Canada, Australia, New Zealand, the UK and EU. Second, what makes India distinctive is the widening linkage of trade with energy, strategic autonomy and geopolitical choices, particularly Russian oil.
Third, the perception of moving goalposts and even the finish line—a concern also articulated by Canada’s Mark Carney—has complicated trust. After reportedly resolving nearly 99 percent of issues, India now seeks certainty that concessions will deliver the February framework’s promised benefits, not another negotiating reset.
VT: Earlier this week, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the two partners had reached a plateau in the negotiations, beyond which it was difficult for either side to offer further concessions. Why did Sitharaman make such a comment?
Dr. Singh: In fact, the trust has weakened between the US and India significantly with President Trump as the US President and it is evident at strategic, operational and tactical levels (QUAD, F404 delays, price-haggling on F414, pressurizing Indian companies to invest in US with tariff threats/trade investigations), limiting India’s willingness to make further concessions. Moreover, Washington’s tactical use of tariffs and tariff threats even during negotiations has reinforced New Delhi’s concerns about policy unpredictability.
Given this scenario, India increasingly wants institutional assurances, not merely tariff concessions—forward-MFN, investor-MFN, sunset and mandatory-review clauses, snap-back provisions and TRQs. Lastly, US tariff actions affecting partners even after concluded agreements have heightened India’s insistence on enforceable safeguards. Thus, Sitharaman’s “plateau” reflects a trust-and-certainty deficit, not simply remaining tariff differences.
VT: Is there anything else that you would like to share with us on this topic
Dr. Singh: The larger issue is the changing global order. US retrenchment from parts of the global landscape, China’s rise and the growing weight of emerging powers are exposing the limits of institutions built around the UN and Bretton Woods architecture.
A perceived drift towards a G2-style US–China condominium also concerns India. For India, the concern is whether Washington sufficiently recognises its core geostrategic interests—energy security, defence autonomy and strategic space. This is increasingly shaping the trade relationship beyond tariffs.

high_priority_articles.title: South Korea's once-hot AI stocks struggle for buyers as doubts grow over memory-chip boom - The Business Times
high_priority_articles.summary: South Korea's once-hot AI stocks struggle for buyers as doubts grow over memory-chip boom  The Business Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Semiconductor hub of Taiwan gaining favour due to its wider and deeper linkages across the AI supply chain
SOUTH Korea spent much of 2026 as a poster child of the scorching global AI trade. Now, by almost every measure, the US$4.3 trillion stock market is rapidly losing relevance with investors.
Turnover has collapsed 70 per cent from its peak in late May, foreigners are retreating at the fastest pace in Asia and local retail investors are also pulling back.
The Kospi, the world’s best-performing major equities benchmark in the first half, has since lost 22 per cent to be the worst in the second half while its AI-heavy Taiwanese and US peers set new highs.
Behind the reversal is a market whose AI fortunes hinge disproportionately on Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the two memory-chip giants at the heart of the global AI supply chain.
That concentration is now a liability as investors question the durability of memory chips’ boom cycle, while the brutal leverage-driven sell-off in the summer has made some global funds hesitant to return.
“The biggest challenge I see for most investors – especially those who only recently got into Korea for the memory chip trade – is that the easy money in that theme has been made,” said Phillip Wool, head of portfolio management at Rayliant Global Advisors, adding his fund has been taking profit in South Korean AI stocks and is now underweight SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics.
The two chipmakers together account for over half of Kospi’s weighting and powered its ascent earlier in 2026. Foreign funds pulled US$131 billion from South Korean stocks this year, the most among major Asian markets, according to exchange data compiled by Bloomberg.
Scepticism over memory chip demand was on full display when shares of Samsung, the world’s top producer of such semiconductors, fell on Thursday (Oct 8) despite a nearly nine-fold surge in quarterly operating profit.
South Korea is now struggling to lure buyers, a problem amplified by the nearing completion of combined 55 trillion won (US$41 billion) stock buybacks by Samsung and SK Hynix.
Repurchases by the two chipmakers accounted for the bulk of the US$23 billion worth of buy orders in the market in September, according to JPMorgan Chase.
“We have seen capital increasingly gravitate back toward US equities, contributing to ongoing foreign outflows from the Korean market,” said Richard Tang, head of research Hong Kong at Julius Baer.
Individual investors, a key force behind Kospi’s 100 per cent rally in the first half, remain elusive following the July rout.
Margin loans outstanding have hovered around 33 trillion won over the past month, after peaking at 38.6 trillion won in June, according to data from the Korea Financial Investment Association. Brokerage account balances – or investor deposits awaiting deployment – have also fallen to around 100 trillion won from a record of near 140 trillion won.
“The memory names in particular have become value names, cheap at current earnings,” said Jon Withaar, a portfolio manager at Pictet Asset Management in Singapore. “But retail and fast money hedge funds do not chase value or the concept ‘cheap’. They chase growth.”
To be sure, the declines have opened up buying opportunities for some investors who see AI spending and memory chip profitability still holding up. South Korea’s ongoing initiative to boost corporate value is also another draw. Thanks to earlier gains, Kospi is still among the best performers for 2026 overall.
Yet for those less convinced, the competing Asian semiconductor hub of Taiwan is gaining favour due to its wider and deeper linkages across the AI supply chain and a more upbeat earnings outlook.
Up 70 per cent in 2026, the Taiex Index beat the Kospi by about 23 percentage points last quarter, the widest margin since the turn of the century. Taiwan’s stock gains are also more broad-based, with about 10 per cent of the local gauge’s members having at least doubled in value this year. That compares to 4.7 per cent for the Kospi.
“At this point in time, we prefer to express our tactical AI exposure through Taiwan equities, which offer a more complete technology hardware ecosystem and are supported by robust spending plans from major technology companies,” said Wu Chun-Lai, head of Asia asset allocation at UBS Global Wealth Management Chief Investment Office. high_priority_articles.summary: Key American industry seeing blue-collar jobs boom as Trump's re-shoring policies pay off  Fox NewsPeter Navarro says gas prices don’t define Trump’s economic record  NewsNationKey American industry seeing blue-collar jobs boom as Trump’s reshoring policies pay off  WFINThe White House releases report on U.S. manufacturing.  Vietnam.vnPeter Navarro to Newsmax: Fox Won't Cover the Trump Economy  Yahoo
high_priority_articles.full_text:
FIRST ON FOX: Critical blue-collar manufacturing jobs in the U.S. are making inroads after years of Biden-era offshoring hollowed out the workforce, according to a new economic report.
A Council of Economic Advisers (CEA) report says 72,000 manufacturing jobs have been added in 2026 alone, many of them due to a rise in the manufacturing of durable goods, like metal and transportation equipment.
The advisors say this is a reverse of a Biden-era trend that saw 200,000 manufacturing jobs disappear in the last two years of the former president's administration.
Not only is the current administration's focus on reshoring jobs contributing to the uptick, but so are his tariff policies, according to the CEA, a White House agency responsible for providing President Donald Trump with economic analysis.
In particular, Trump's landmark One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBB) has laid the groundwork for American companies to expand in the United States, instead of shipping jobs overseas, according to the report. The bill's provisions include allowing manufacturers an immediate 100% tax deduction on expenses related to new factory building and purchasing machinery and equipment.
The report highlights success stories from corporations reinvesting in Americans and expanding their businesses.
For example, the 100% expensing provision in the OBBB has helped Jergens, a manufacturing company based in Ohio, expand to Illinois.
"Since the passage of the bill [OBBB], our employees are voluntarily working additional hours," the company's CEO, Jack Schron, said. "They are keeping more of what they earn, putting more money back into the American economy, and Jergens has a ready workforce. It is a win-win-win: a win for the employee, for Jergens and for the United States economy."
Schron added that 83% of his workers are picking up overtime after the OBBB provision established no taxes for overtime work.
In another example touted in the CEA report, a company in North Carolina, Ketchie Inc., has expanded its workforce by 25% after taking advantage of the 100% expensing provision to purchase new machinery. The report says the company waited to buy the equipment until the OBBB passed.
As for wages, manufacturing workers are seeing benefits, too, with their pay increasing by 7.9% since January 2025.
"Adjusted for inflation, this means that blue-collar manufacturing workers are earning nearly $2,500 more per year, on average, since President Trump took office," the report says.
It also touts figures from the construction industry, including 100,000 construction jobs added since Trump took office.
Semiconductor chip manufacturing, an industry in which the United States typically competes with China, is on the rise in the United States too.
Micron is building memory chip plants in Idaho, Virginia and New York, which the report says is a $250 billion investment in the United States. Apple is investing $600 billion in American semiconductor production, too.
The report also says that major pharmaceutical companies like GSK and Gilead are investing billions of dollars in the United States, along with automakers like Stellantis.
All told, the reshoring and tariff policies have resulted in $11 trillion in investments in the United States during Trump's second term in office, according to the report.
Meanwhile, the economy is on everyone's mind with only a few weeks left until the midterm elections. Inflation, particularly high gas and grocery prices, continue to impact Americans before they head to the polls.
According to a Fox News Poll, the cost of everyday items is a hardship for voters: 61% say gas prices are a major problem, up from 48% two years ago, while 52% say the same for healthcare costs, up from 44%. Majorities also view housing costs (54%, down from 60%) and grocery prices (62%, down from 66%) as major problems.
Nearly two-thirds of Americans say the economy is worse under the Trump administration than before.
